newsitem.title: USA: U.S. May air cargo trade rises says Tokyo-Mitsubis.
newsitem.headline: U.S. May air cargo trade rises says Tokyo-Mitsubis.

text.p: The index of U.S. air cargo trade activity rose 2.0 percent in May after a flat reading in April, Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi said.

In its latest Foreign Trade survey of air freight carriers, seaports and trucking firms, the bank said its air cargo index increased to 495.2 from 485.4 in the prior month. Imports led the way, as they have for most of this year.

The air cargo current-conditions import index rose 4.1 percent to 499.9 in May, it's second-strongest 1997 showing after March's 7.4 percent surge. Meanwhile, the export index was unchanged at 490.4 after an even two percent April decline.
"A strong U.S. economy again helped fuel imports," Michael Niemira, a Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi economist, told Reuters.

However, he said industry expectations are that "the dollar's relative performance and a slower-growing domestic economy may evaporate mini-booms seen this year in imports and, to a far lesser degree, exports."

Reflecting these concerns, the bank's index of future air cargo business, which had averaged a 1.3 percent monthly advance over January-April, registered a 0.5 percent decline in May. This measure had risen 0.9 percent in April.
Taking a longer term perspective, the economist said the picture may be more positive.
"Until the 1995 U.S. economic slowdown, air cargo exports and imports both were booming," Niemira observed, "but then there was a dramatic slowing through the low reached late in 1996."
However, he said "now the trend seems to be turning around on both fronts."
Special industries are the main contributors, in Niemira's estimation. Aircraft deliveries to foreigners are higher by one billion dollars per month over last year and apparel imports are booming.
He added that the U.S. economy posted strong growth in Q4-1996 and Q1-1997 to help suck in imports and exports have been assisted by some strengthening in European economies.

"The air cargo industry still is underperforming the growth in the goods industry overall," Niemira observed, adding that this reflects the focus on high-value, technology goods shipped by air as opposed to the overall universe of goods.
Within the cargo sector, exports are relatively stronger than imports when compared to the overall universe of goods imports and exports.
Air imports are running at about a six percent annual growth pace (on a three-month average annualized basis), while overall goods imports are growing at around 10 percent.
In contrast to this four percentage point difference, there is less of a gap between air-shipped and other exports.
Export air cargo is expanding at about five percent versus an eight to 8.5 percent pace for overall exports.

Interestingly, Niemira estimated that in the high-tech merchandise area (such as computers and similar things) of goods shipped by air, the United States actually is running a surplus of around 800 million dollars compared with an overall merchandise trade deficit of roughly 15 billion dollars.

The bank's data show that its index for air cargo export business fell an even one percent to 604.0 in May from 610.0 in the prior month. On the same basis, the index for export expectations declined 1.4 percent to 660.7.
The air cargo import business index advanced 1.7 percent to 446.6 in May from 439.0 in the prior month. The index for air cargo import expectations rose 0.9 percent to 445.5.
The basic index (1989=100) is an equally-weighted composite index of current U.S. export and import air cargo activity that is not seasonally adjusted.

On the basis of an alternate presentation using not-seasonally-adjusted diffusion indexes, the air cargo current conditions export diffusion index for May stood at 50.0 percent. That was the weakest May reading since 1991.
